questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(2y+3x)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2y+3x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+3)-(-2+0) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }$, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta } \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\frac{4{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4({cos}^{2}⁡2\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4([\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos^2\theta$ and $y=\cos\theta \sin{\theta}$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}4.$

Now, if $f(x,y) =y^2-x$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \text{ }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta (-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-x)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{y^2}$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\leq \theta \leq \dfrac\pi 2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta$, where $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}2.$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2+y^2}{y^2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-(0-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos^2\theta$ and $y=\cos\theta\sin\theta$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = xy(1-x^2)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}) \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\cos\theta,$ $\textrm d u=-\sin\theta\,\textrm d \theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{1}^{0}-{u}^{3}(1-{u}^{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{3}-{u}^{7})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{u}^{8}}{8}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
